title: Rate limiter design
idea: A rate limiter decides, per client, whether one more request is allowed now, so no client can send more than a set number in a period.

analogy.text: An arcade card holds at most three game credits and gains one each minute. Each game spends a credit. No credit, no game until the next one arrives.
analogy.breaks: A card can be topped up with money; a bucket refills only with time.

points: Callers depend on one `RateLimiter` interface; each algorithm is a separate class.
Token bucket allows short bursts up to capacity, then a steady refill rate.
Fixed windows are cheap, but allow a double burst across a window boundary.
Inject the clock as a `TimeSource`, and make `tryAcquire` atomic with `synchronized`.

code: refill();  // add earned tokens, cap at 3

steps.caption: The bucket starts full with three tokens. Four requests arrive at the same instant.
Request 1 finds a token, spends it and is allowed.
Requests 2 and 3 spend the last two tokens. A burst of three is fine.
Request 4 finds the bucket empty. `tryAcquire` returns `false` and nothing changes.
One second later, the next call to `refill` adds one earned token.
Request 5 spends it. After a burst, the steady rate is one per second.
After a long quiet spell, refill stops at capacity. Idle time never buys a bigger burst.

code.title: Token bucket
code.caption: A manual clock drives the bucket, so every run prints the same decisions.

walk.text: Time is a dependency. A `ManualClock` lets tests and demos move it by hand.
The contract callers see. Swapping the algorithm changes no caller.
The bucket starts full and remembers when it last refilled.
Whole tokens earned since the last refill are added, capped at capacity.
Spend one token or refuse. `synchronized` makes refill and spend one step.
Four at time 0, then later calls. At 9000 the bucket holds only three.

code.title: Fixed vs sliding window
code.caption: Same limit, two per second, same requests. Watch what happens around the 1000 ms boundary.

walk.text: A per-client contract: the caller passes client id and time. A token bucket needs one bucket per id.
Fixed window: round time down to the window start, reset the count when it changes.
Sliding log: drop timestamps older than one window, then count what remains.
Count what each allows between 900 and 1050. Client u2 has its own log.

pitfalls: Do not call `System.currentTimeMillis()` inside the limiter; inject a clock so tests are exact.
Make refill, check and spend one atomic step, or concurrent calls overspend tokens.
Evict state for idle clients; one entry per client id grows without bound otherwise.

quiz.why: Fixed window resets its count at 1000, so it allows. The sliding log still holds 900 and 950, two requests within one second, so it refuses.

takeaway: One limiter interface, an injected clock, and an atomic check-and-spend.

starters: Which rate limiting algorithm should I pick in an interview, and why?
How would this work across many servers sharing one limit?
How does a sliding window counter save memory compared with a log?
